items.stem: Which equation is used to calculate density?
items.answer: density = mass ÷ volume
items.markingKey: Density is mass per unit volume.

items.stem: A block of wood and a block of iron have the same mass. Explain which has the larger volume.
items.answer: The wood, because it is less dense; for the same mass a lower density means a larger volume.
items.markingKey: wood [1]; lower density so larger volume [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a steel ship floats although steel is denser than water.
items.answer: The ship is hollow and contains air, so its average density (total mass ÷ total volume) is less than that of water.
items.markingKey: hollow / contains air [1]; average density less than water [1] [2]

items.stem: A cuboid cut from oak wood has a mass of 37.5 g and a volume of 50 cm³. Determine the density in g/cm³.
items.answer: 0.75 g/cm³
items.markingKey: ρ = m/V = 37.5 / 50 = 0.75 g/cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A rectangular block of lead measures 2 cm × 2 cm × 2 cm and has a mass of 90.4 g. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
items.answer: 11.3 g/cm³

items.stem: A metal sample in a school laboratory is a cuboid 4 cm by 2.5 cm by 1 cm, with a mass of 27 g. (a) Calculate its density in g/cm³. (b) State and explain whether it would float in milk of density 1.03 g/cm³.
items.answer: (a) 2.7 g/cm³ (b) Sinks: its density is greater than 1.03 g/cm³.
items.markingKey: (a) ρ = m/V = 27/10 = 2.7 g/cm³ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.7 g/cm³ with unit [1] [2] (b) Sinks [1]; its density is greater than 1.03 g/cm³ [1] [2]

items.stem: Which unit could be used for density?
items.answer: g/cm³
items.markingKey: Mass in g ÷ volume in cm³ gives g/cm³ (or kg/m³).

items.stem: Explain, using the particle model, why most substances are less dense as gases than as solids.
items.answer: The same particles (same mass) are much further apart in a gas, so the volume is much bigger and density is lower.
items.markingKey: same mass [1]; particles far apart / larger volume [1] [2]

items.stem: A cuboid cut from silver has a mass of 1050 g and a volume of 100 cm³. What is the density in g/cm³?
items.answer: 10.5 g/cm³

items.stem: Isla finds the mass of a broken fragment of iron is 119 g. The water in a measuring cylinder reads 60 cm³ before and 75 cm³ after the object is fully submerged. Calculate the density in kg/m³.
items.answer: 7900 kg/m³

items.stem: In which unit is temperature usually measured in the laboratory?
items.answer: degrees Celsius (°C)
items.markingKey: Temperature in °C, measured with a thermometer.

items.stem: Explain the difference between heat (thermal energy) and temperature.
items.answer: Thermal energy is the total energy of all the particles, measured in J; temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles, measured in °C.
items.markingKey: thermal energy = total energy (J) [1]; temperature = average energy of particles (°C) [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a swimming pool at 25 °C contains more thermal energy than a cup of coffee at 75 °C.
items.answer: The pool has a much larger mass (many more particles); total energy depends on mass as well as temperature.
items.markingKey: much greater mass / more particles [1]; total energy depends on mass and temperature [1] [2]

items.stem: Leila measures the temperature of a mug of hot soup as it cools in a room at 28 °C: 0 min: 85 °C, 4 min: 66 °C, 8 min: 54 °C, 12 min: 45 °C, 16 min: 40 °C, 20 min: 36 °C. Calculate the fall in temperature in the first 4 minutes and in the last 4 minutes.
items.answer: 19 °C and 4 °C

items.stem: Mateo measures the temperature of a cup of tea as it cools in a room at 18 °C: 0 min: 80 °C, 4 min: 67 °C, 8 min: 56 °C, 12 min: 48 °C, 16 min: 42 °C, 20 min: 37 °C. (a) Calculate the temperature fall in the first 4 minutes and in the last 4 minutes. (b) Explain why the drink cools more slowly later on.
items.answer: (a) 13 °C and 5 °C (b) The temperature difference between the drink and the room gets smaller, so thermal energy is transferred more slowly.
items.markingKey: (a) 13 and 5 °C [1] (b) smaller temperature difference [1]; slower transfer of energy [1] [3]

items.stem: A can of cold drink at 10 °C is placed in a bowl of hot water at 60 °C. The room is at 22 °C. (a) Explain why the final temperature of both objects will be the same. (b) Explain why, after a long time, both end up at 22 °C.
items.answer: (a) Energy transfers until there is no temperature difference; then there is no net transfer (thermal equilibrium). (b) The water also loses energy to the cooler room until everything reaches room temperature, 22 °C.
items.markingKey: (a) transfer until equal temperature [1]; no net transfer after [1] [2] (b) energy lost to surroundings [1]; reaches 22 °C [1] [2]

items.stem: A cup of hot chocolate is left on a table. Explain why it cools down and then stops cooling.
items.answer: Thermal energy moves from the hot drink to the cooler surroundings until the drink reaches room temperature; then there is no temperature difference so no net transfer.
items.markingKey: energy flows hot → cold [1]; stops at room temperature / no difference [1] [2]

items.stem: Mohammed says: "Heat and temperature mean the same thing." Explain why Mohammed is wrong.
items.answer: Thermal energy (heat) is total energy in joules; temperature measures average particle energy in °C.
items.markingKey: distinguish energy (J) [1]; temperature (°C) [1] [2]

items.stem: Lucas measures the temperature of a mug of hot soup as it cools in a room at 18 °C: 0 min: 70 °C, 4 min: 59 °C, 8 min: 50 °C, 12 min: 43 °C, 16 min: 38 °C, 20 min: 34 °C. What will the temperature of the drink be after a very long time?
items.markingKey: It cools until it reaches room temperature, 18 °C.

items.stem: Ines puts a metal block at 5 °C into a beaker of water at 80 °C on a bench in a laboratory in Cape Town, where the air is at 25 °C. (a) Explain why the final temperature of both objects will be the same. (b) Suggest how to measure the temperatures accurately.
items.answer: (a) Energy transfers until there is no temperature difference; then there is no net transfer (thermal equilibrium). (b) Use a thermometer or temperature probe, stir the water, read at eye level and wait for the reading to become steady.
items.markingKey: (a) transfer until equal temperature [1]; no net transfer after [1] [2] (b) any two good points [1] each [2]

items.stem: Which statement is the law of conservation of energy?
options: Energy is used up when a device works
Energy is destroyed as thermal energy
Energy can be created by machines
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or stored
items.answer: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or stored
items.markingKey: Total energy stays the same; it is only transferred between stores.

items.stem: Explain why a car engine gets hot when it is running.
items.answer: Not all the chemical energy from the fuel is transferred to kinetic energy; some is dissipated as thermal energy because of friction and the burning fuel.
items.markingKey: not all energy useful [1]; dissipated as thermal energy (friction / burning) [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how lubricating the moving parts of a bicycle reduces energy dissipation.
items.answer: Oil reduces friction between moving parts, so less energy is transferred as thermal energy and sound.
items.markingKey: less friction [1]; less thermal energy and sound wasted [1] [2]

items.stem: A kettle is supplied with 400 J of electrical energy and transfers 360 J as useful thermal energy of the water. Calculate the energy dissipated and state the main form of the wasted energy.
items.answer: 40 J, mainly as thermal energy of the surroundings and sound
items.markingKey: 400 − 360 = 40 J [1]; thermal energy of the surroundings and sound [1] [2]

items.stem: An LED lamp is supplied with 1200 J of electrical energy and transfers 480 J as useful light. (a) Calculate the energy dissipated. (b) Calculate the percentage of the input energy that is useful.

An LED lamp transfers 41.7 J of energy every second. In 60 s it transfers 1250 J usefully as light. (a) Calculate the total energy supplied in 60 s. (b) Calculate the energy dissipated. (c) Calculate the percentage of the energy that is wasted.

An electric motor in a home in Bangkok is supplied with 1000 J of energy. 600 J is transferred usefully as kinetic energy. (a) Calculate the energy wasted. (b) Draw or describe an energy flow (Sankey) diagram for the device. (c) Suggest one way to reduce the wasted energy.
items.answer: (a) 400 J (b) An arrow 1000 J wide splitting into a useful arrow of 600 J (kinetic energy) and a wasted arrow of 400 J; widths in proportion. (c) Reduce friction by lubrication, use insulation, or use a more efficient design (e.g. LED).
items.markingKey: (a) 1000 − 600 = 400 J: 400 J [1] (b) input splits into useful and wasted [1]; widths in proportion and labelled [1] [2] (c) Reduce friction by lubrication, use insulation, or use a more efficient design (e.g. LED) [1]

items.stem: A solar cell in a home in Lisbon is supplied with 2500 J of energy. 375 J is transferred usefully as electrical. (a) Calculate the energy wasted. (b) Name the main form of the wasted energy and where it goes. (c) Explain how the total energy output compares with the energy supplied.
items.answer: (a) 2130 J (b) Thermal energy, spreading into the surroundings. (c) They are equal: energy is conserved, so useful + wasted = input.
items.markingKey: (a) 2500 − 375 = 2130 J: 2130 J [1] (b) form [1]; surroundings [1] [2] (c) equal [1]; conservation of energy [1] [2]

items.stem: What is meant by “dissipated” energy?
options: Energy that spreads out into the surroundings and is less useful
Energy that increases the useful output
Energy that is stored in a battery
items.answer: Energy that spreads out into the surroundings and is less useful
items.markingKey: Dissipated energy is wasted energy, usually spread out as thermal energy in the surroundings.

items.stem: Explain why LED lamps are replacing filament lamps.
items.answer: An LED transfers a much larger proportion of its input energy to light, so less is dissipated as heat; it needs less energy for the same light.
items.markingKey: more light per joule / less wasted heat [1]; uses less energy for same light [1] [2]

items.stem: Aisha claims: "The bouncing ball loses energy so the total energy decreases." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. The ball’s energy decreases, but the energy is transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy and sound; total energy stays the same.
items.markingKey: energy transferred not lost [1]; total conserved [1] [2]

items.stem: Omar drops a table-tennis ball from a height of 2 m. It bounces back up to 1.4 m. Explain why the ball does not return to its starting height.
items.answer: At the bounce some energy is dissipated as thermal energy (and sound), so the ball has less energy and less gravitational potential energy at the top.
items.markingKey: energy transferred to thermal / sound [1]; less GPE so lower height [1] [2]

items.stem: A loudspeaker in a home in Dhaka is supplied with 2000 J of energy. 100 J is transferred usefully as sound. (a) Draw or describe an energy flow (Sankey) diagram for the device. (b) Explain how the total energy output compares with the energy supplied. (c) Suggest one way to reduce the wasted energy.
items.answer: (a) An arrow 2000 J wide splitting into a useful arrow of 100 J (sound) and a wasted arrow of 1900 J; widths in proportion. (b) They are equal: energy is conserved, so useful + wasted = input. (c) Reduce friction by lubrication, use insulation, or use a more efficient design (e.g. LED).
items.markingKey: (a) input splits into useful and wasted [1]; widths in proportion and labelled [1] [2] (b) equal [1]; conservation of energy [1] [2] (c) Reduce friction by lubrication, use insulation, or use a more efficient design (e.g. LED) [1]

items.stem: In which state of matter does conduction mainly take place?
items.answer: Solids
items.markingKey: Particles in solids are close together and pass vibrations on.

items.stem: Explain how a convection current forms in a pan of water heated from below.
items.answer: Water at the bottom is heated, expands and becomes less dense so it rises; cooler, denser water sinks to take its place, forming a circulating current.
items.markingKey: heated water expands / less dense [1]; rises [1]; cooler denser water sinks [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why metals are good conductors of thermal energy.
items.answer: They have free electrons that move quickly and carry energy, as well as vibrating particles passing energy to neighbours.
items.markingKey: free electrons carry energy [1]; vibrations passed on [1] [2]

items.stem: Omar fixes a drawing pin with wax to the end of rods of different metals, all the same length and thickness. The other ends are heated equally. Times for the pins to fall: steel 60 s, brass 27 s, copper 8 s, iron 38 s. Put the metals in order from best to worst conductor and explain how you decided.
items.answer: copper, brass, iron, steel; the shorter the time for the pin to fall, the faster energy is conducted.
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; shorter time = better conductor [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas fixes a drawing pin with wax to the end of rods of different metals, all the same length and thickness. The other ends are heated equally. Times for the pins to fall: iron 38 s, steel 60 s, brass 27 s, copper 8 s. (a) Put the metals in order from best to worst conductor. (b) Name two variables that must be kept the same. (c) Explain, in terms of particles, how energy travels along the rod.
items.answer: (a) copper, brass, iron, steel (b) Length and thickness of the rods (or amount of wax, distance of pin, heating). (c) Particles at the hot end vibrate more and pass energy to neighbouring particles; free electrons also carry energy along.
items.markingKey: (a) order [1] (b) two control variables [1] (c) vibrating particles pass energy on [1] [3]

items.stem: A family in Karachi wants to keep their home warm in winter and cool in summer. (a) Explain how loft insulation made of fibre reduces energy loss. (b) Explain why a room heater is usually placed low down near the floor.
items.answer: (a) The fibres trap air, which is a poor conductor and cannot circulate, so conduction and convection through the roof are reduced. (b) Air warmed by the heater becomes less dense and rises, and cooler air sinks to replace it, setting up a convection current around the room.
items.markingKey: (a) traps air [1]; reduces conduction and convection [1] [2] (b) warm air rises [1]; convection current [1] [2]

items.stem: Sipho claims: "Shiny surfaces are good at absorbing radiation." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. Shiny surfaces reflect most infrared and are poor absorbers; dull black surfaces are the best absorbers.
items.markingKey: shiny reflects [1]; dull black best absorber [1] [2]

items.stem: Aisha fills three identical metal cans, painted different colours, with water at 75 °C. After 10 minutes the temperatures are: shiny silver can: 66 °C, shiny white can: 61 °C, dull black can: 49 °C. Calculate the fall in temperature of the shiny silver can and state which surface emits radiation best.
items.answer: 9 °C; dull black

items.stem: Daniel fixes a drawing pin with wax to the end of rods of different metals, all the same length and thickness. The other ends are heated equally. Times for the pins to fall: steel 96 s, iron 60 s, copper 12 s, brass 44 s. (a) Put the metals in order from best to worst conductor. (b) Name two variables that must be kept the same. (c) Explain, in terms of particles, how energy travels along the rod. (d) Suggest which metal should be used for the base of a cooking pan and why.
items.answer: (a) copper, brass, iron, steel (b) Length and thickness of the rods (or amount of wax, distance of pin, heating). (c) Particles at the hot end vibrate more and pass energy to neighbouring particles; free electrons also carry energy along. (d) Copper, because it conducts energy to the food fastest (copper bases spread heat evenly).
items.markingKey: (a) order [1] (b) two control variables [1] (c) vibrating particles pass energy on [1]; free electrons [1] (d) best conductor with reason [1] [5]

items.stem: A family in Istanbul wants to keep their home warm in winter and cool in summer. (a) Explain how loft insulation made of fibre reduces energy loss. (b) Suggest why light-coloured curtains help keep the house cool in summer.
items.answer: (a) The fibres trap air, which is a poor conductor and cannot circulate, so conduction and convection through the roof are reduced. (b) Light colours reflect infrared radiation from the Sun, so less energy is absorbed into the room.
items.markingKey: (a) traps air [1]; reduces conduction and convection [1] [2] (b) reflect radiation [1]; less absorbed [1] [2]

items.stem: Which particles escape from the surface of a liquid during evaporation?
options: Particles from the bottom of the liquid
The particles with the least energy
The particles with the most energy
items.answer: The particles with the most energy
items.markingKey: The fastest-moving particles near the surface escape.

items.stem: Why does a liquid cool when it evaporates?
options: The liquid absorbs cold from the air
The particles left behind have a lower average energy
The particles left behind gain energy
items.answer: The particles left behind have a lower average energy
items.markingKey: Losing the most energetic particles lowers the average kinetic energy, so temperature falls.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of particles, why evaporation cools a liquid.
items.answer: The most energetic particles escape from the surface, so the average kinetic energy of those left falls, and the temperature drops.
items.markingKey: most energetic escape [1]; average energy of remaining falls [1] [2]

items.stem: Mei places two thermometers in a room at 22 °C. The bulb of thermometer B is wrapped in cotton wool soaked in water; thermometer A is dry. After 10 minutes A reads 22 °C and B reads 16 °C. A fan is then switched on and B falls to 12 °C. Calculate the extra cooling caused by the fan and explain it.
items.answer: 4 °C; the moving air removes vapour so the water evaporates faster, removing energy faster.
items.markingKey: 10 − 6 = 4 °C [1]; faster evaporation in moving air [1] [2]

items.stem: A shop in Lagos uses an evaporative cooler: a fan blows hot air at 38 °C through wet pads, and the air comes out at about 24 °C. (a) Calculate the temperature drop produced. (b) Explain why the cooler must be refilled with water regularly.
items.answer: (a) 14 °C (b) Water is continually lost by evaporation; without water no evaporation, so no cooling.
items.markingKey: (a) 38 − 24 = 14 °C: 14 °C [1] (b) water evaporates away [1]; no water no cooling [1] [2]

items.stem: Grace places two thermometers in a room at 26 °C. The bulb of thermometer B is wrapped in cotton wool soaked in water; thermometer A is dry. After 8 minutes A reads 26 °C and B reads 22 °C. A fan is then switched on and B falls to 19 °C. (a) Explain why thermometer B reads lower than A. (b) Explain why the fan lowers the reading further. (c) Explain why thermometer A is included.
items.answer: (a) Evaporation from the wet cotton removes the most energetic particles, so energy is taken from the bulb. (b) The fan carries vapour away so evaporation is faster. (c) It is a control, showing the room temperature.
items.markingKey: (a) evaporation removes energy [1] (b) faster evaporation [1] (c) control / comparison [1] [3]

items.stem: In hot, dry areas near Cape Town, people keep vegetables in a “pot-in-pot” cooler: a small clay pot inside a larger one, with wet sand between them. On a day at 38 °C, the inner pot stays at about 24 °C. (a) Calculate the temperature drop produced. (b) Explain, using ideas about particles, how the cooler works. (c) Explain why the cooler works better in dry air than in humid air.
items.answer: (a) 14 °C (b) Water evaporates; the most energetic water particles escape, so the average energy of what remains falls and thermal energy is taken from the inside / the air. (c) Dry air contains little water vapour so evaporation is faster, giving more cooling.
items.markingKey: (a) 38 − 24 = 14 °C: 14 °C [1] (b) evaporation [1]; most energetic particles leave [1]; energy taken from inside / air [1] [3] (c) dry air faster evaporation [1]; more cooling [1] [2]

items.stem: The density of water is 1.0 g/cm³. Which object will float in water?
options: A block of wood of density 0.7 g/cm³
A steel nail of density 7.8 g/cm³
A glass marble of density 2.5 g/cm³
items.answer: A block of wood of density 0.7 g/cm³
items.markingKey: Objects less dense than water float.

items.stem: Explain why ice floats on water.
items.answer: Ice is less dense than liquid water, because water expands when it freezes.
items.markingKey: ice less dense [1]; water expands on freezing [1] [2]

items.stem: Freya finds that a lump of gold has a mass of 96.5 g. It is lowered into a measuring cylinder and the water level rises from 40 cm³ to 45 cm³. Calculate the density of the object.
items.answer: 19.3 g/cm³
items.markingKey: V = 45 − 40 = 5 cm³; ρ = 96.5/5 = 19.3 g/cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Lucas is given a cuboid of an unknown material measuring 3 cm × 2.5 cm × 3 cm. Its mass is 60.8 g. (a) Calculate its density in g/cm³. (b) A second block of the same material has twice the length, width and height. State its density and its mass.
items.answer: (a) 2.7 g/cm³ (b) Density unchanged at 2.7 g/cm³; mass = 8 × 60.8 = 486 g.
items.markingKey: (a) ρ = m/V = 60.8/22.5 = 2.7 g/cm³ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.7 g/cm³ with unit [1] [2] (b) density same [1]; volume ×8 so mass ×8 [1] [2]

items.stem: In which unit is thermal energy measured?
items.answer: joules (J)
items.markingKey: Energy, including thermal energy, is measured in joules.

items.stem: Describe what happens to the particles of a metal spoon when it is placed in hot water.
items.answer: The particles gain energy and vibrate faster, so the temperature of the spoon rises.
items.markingKey: particles gain energy [1]; vibrate faster / temperature rises [1] [2]

items.stem: Mei mixes 150 g of water at 24 °C with 150 g of water at 80 °C in an insulated cup. Assuming no energy is lost, calculate the final temperature and explain your answer.
items.answer: 52 °C; the hot water loses as much energy as the cold water gains, and as the masses are equal the temperature change is the same for both.
items.markingKey: 52 °C [1]; energy lost by hot = energy gained by cold [1] [2]

items.stem: Ana puts a metal block at 8 °C into a beaker of water at 70 °C on a bench in a laboratory in Dhaka, where the air is at 25 °C. (a) State the direction in which thermal energy is transferred between the two objects. (b) Describe what happens to the movement of the particles in each object. (c) Explain why, after a long time, both end up at 25 °C.
items.answer: (a) From the hot water to the colder object. (b) Particles in the colder object speed up (gain energy); particles in the hot water slow down (lose energy). (c) The water also loses energy to the cooler room until everything reaches room temperature, 25 °C.
items.markingKey: (a) From the hot water to the colder object [1] (b) cold object particles speed up [1]; hot water particles slow down [1] [2] (c) energy lost to surroundings [1]; reaches 25 °C [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which energy store decreases when a ball falls? (b) What is meant by “dissipated” energy?
items.answer: (a) Gravitational potential energy (b) Energy that spreads out into the surroundings and is less useful
items.markingKey: (a) As it falls, gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy. (b) Dissipated energy is wasted energy, usually spread out as thermal energy in the surroundings.

items.stem: A swinging pendulum gradually comes to rest. Explain where its energy has gone.
items.answer: Its energy is transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy by air resistance and friction at the pivot; the total energy is conserved but spread out.
items.markingKey: air resistance / friction [1]; thermal energy in surroundings, not destroyed [1] [2]

items.stem: A filament lamp is supplied with 400 J of electrical energy and transfers 40 J as useful light. Calculate the energy dissipated and state the main form of the wasted energy.
items.answer: 360 J, mainly as thermal energy in the surroundings
items.markingKey: 400 − 40 = 360 J [1]; thermal energy in the surroundings [1] [2]

items.stem: Sofia drops a tennis ball from a height of 3 m. It bounces back up to 2.25 m. (a) Describe the energy changes from the moment of release to the top of the bounce. (b) The gravitational potential energy is proportional to height. Calculate the percentage of the original energy the ball still has at the top of the bounce.
items.answer: (a) Gravitational potential → kinetic as it falls; at impact some kinetic is dissipated as thermal and sound, and some stored as elastic energy then back to kinetic; kinetic → gravitational potential as it rises. (b) 2.25 ÷ 3 × 100 = 75%
items.markingKey: (a) GPE → KE [1]; dissipation at bounce [1] (b) 2.25 ÷ 3 × 100 = 75% [1] [3]

items.stem: A car engine is supplied with 400 J of chemical energy of the fuel and transfers 120 J as useful kinetic energy. (a) Calculate the energy dissipated. (b) Calculate the percentage of the input energy that is useful.
Explain why houses in hot countries are often painted white.
items.answer: White surfaces reflect most infrared radiation and absorb little, so the house heats up less.
items.markingKey: white reflects radiation [1]; absorbs less so stays cooler [1] [2]

items.stem: Lucas says: "Heat rises." Explain why Lucas is wrong.
items.answer: Hot fluids (air or water) rise because they are less dense; thermal energy itself can move in any direction, e.g. by conduction or radiation downwards.
items.markingKey: it is hot fluid that rises (density) [1]; energy can travel in any direction [1] [2]

items.stem: Lina fixes a drawing pin with wax to the end of rods of different metals, all the same length and thickness. The other ends are heated equally. Times for the pins to fall: steel 48 s, brass 22 s, iron 30 s, copper 6 s. Put the metals in order from best to worst conductor and explain how you decided.
items.answer: copper, brass, iron, steel; the shorter the time for the pin to fall, the faster energy is conducted.
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; shorter time = better conductor [1] [2]

items.stem: A family in Dhaka wants to keep their home warm in winter and cool in summer. (a) Explain how double glazing reduces energy transfer. (b) Explain why a room heater is usually placed low down near the floor. (c) Suggest why light-coloured curtains help keep the house cool in summer.
items.answer: (a) The gap between the panes contains air or a vacuum; air is a poor conductor and the narrow gap limits convection. (b) Air warmed by the heater becomes less dense and rises, and cooler air sinks to replace it, setting up a convection current around the room. (c) Light colours reflect infrared radiation from the Sun, so less energy is absorbed into the room.
items.markingKey: (a) gap with air / vacuum [1]; poor conductor / limited convection [1] [2] (b) warm air rises [1]; convection current [1] [2] (c) reflect radiation [1]; less absorbed [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why you feel cold when you get out of a swimming pool on a windy day.
items.answer: Water on your skin evaporates quickly in the wind, taking thermal energy from your skin.
items.markingKey: evaporation [1]; wind increases rate / energy taken from skin [1] [2]

items.stem: Aisha places two thermometers in a room at 24 °C. The bulb of thermometer B is wrapped in cotton wool soaked in water; thermometer A is dry. After 5 minutes A reads 24 °C and B reads 21 °C. A fan is then switched on and B falls to 19 °C. Calculate the extra cooling caused by the fan and explain it.
items.answer: 2 °C; the moving air removes vapour so the water evaporates faster, removing energy faster.
items.markingKey: 5 − 3 = 2 °C [1]; faster evaporation in moving air [1] [2]

items.stem: A shop in Nairobi uses an evaporative cooler: a fan blows hot air at 32 °C through wet pads, and the air comes out at about 18 °C. (a) Suggest why the cooler works better when placed in a breeze. (b) Evaluate one advantage and one disadvantage of this cooler compared with an electric refrigerator.
items.answer: (a) Moving air removes water vapour from the surface so evaporation continues faster. (b) Advantage: needs no electricity, cheap. Disadvantage: cannot reach very low temperatures and works poorly in humid weather; needs water.
items.markingKey: (a) breeze removes vapour [1]; faster evaporation [1] [2] (b) advantage [1]; disadvantage [1] [2]

items.stem: Which method is used to find the volume of an irregular stone?
options: Displacement of water in a measuring cylinder
Measuring its length, width and height
Timing how long it takes to sink
items.answer: Displacement of water in a measuring cylinder
items.markingKey: The rise in water level equals the volume of the stone.

items.stem: Explain why a hot-air balloon rises.
items.answer: Heating the air makes it expand so it becomes less dense than the cooler air around it; the less dense balloon rises.
items.markingKey: hot air expands / less dense [1]; less dense than surrounding air so rises [1] [2]

items.stem: 80 cm³ of ethanol has a mass of 63.2 g. Determine the density of ethanol.
items.answer: 0.79 g/cm³
items.markingKey: ρ = 63.2/80 = 0.79 g/cm³. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A metal sample in a school laboratory is a cuboid 4 cm by 5 cm by 2 cm, with a mass of 316 g. (a) Calculate its density in g/cm³. (b) A second block of the same material has twice the length, width and height. State its density and its mass.
items.answer: (a) 7.9 g/cm³ (b) Density unchanged at 7.9 g/cm³; mass = 8 × 316 = 2530 g.
items.markingKey: (a) ρ = m/V = 316/40 = 7.9 g/cm³ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 7.9 g/cm³ with unit [1] [2] (b) density same [1]; volume ×8 so mass ×8 [1] [2]

items.stem: Thermal energy always moves …
options: from a larger object to a smaller object
from a cooler object to a hotter object
from a hotter object to a cooler object
items.answer: from a hotter object to a cooler object
items.markingKey: Energy transfers from hot to cold until temperatures are equal.

items.stem: Explain why holding an ice cube makes your hand feel cold.
items.answer: Thermal energy moves from your warmer hand into the ice, so your hand loses energy and its temperature falls.
items.markingKey: energy from hand to ice [1]; hand cools [1] [2]

items.stem: Lina measures the temperature of a flask lid of coffee as it cools in a room at 28 °C: 0 min: 90 °C, 5 min: 74 °C, 10 min: 62 °C, 15 min: 53 °C, 20 min: 47 °C, 25 min: 42 °C. Calculate the fall in temperature in the first 5 minutes and in the last 5 minutes.
items.answer: 16 °C and 5 °C

items.stem: Mohammed puts a metal block at 10 °C into a beaker of water at 80 °C on a bench in a laboratory in Cairo, where the air is at 22 °C. (a) State the direction in which thermal energy is transferred between the two objects. (b) Describe what happens to the movement of the particles in each object. (c) Explain why the final temperature of both objects will be the same.
items.answer: (a) From the hot water to the colder object. (b) Particles in the colder object speed up (gain energy); particles in the hot water slow down (lose energy). (c) Energy transfers until there is no temperature difference; then there is no net transfer (thermal equilibrium).
items.markingKey: (a) From the hot water to the colder object [1] (b) cold object particles speed up [1]; hot water particles slow down [1] [2] (c) transfer until equal temperature [1]; no net transfer after [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which energy store decreases when a ball falls? (b) Which statement is the law of conservation of energy?
items.answer: (a) Gravitational potential energy (b) Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or stored
items.markingKey: (a) As it falls, gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy. (b) Total energy stays the same; it is only transferred between stores.

items.stem: Explain why dissipated energy is difficult to use again.
items.answer: It is spread out thinly into the surroundings at a low temperature, so it cannot easily be collected to do useful work.
items.markingKey: spread out [1]; low temperature / hard to collect [1] [2]

items.stem: Ravi drops a tennis ball from a height of 2.4 m. It bounces back up to 1.92 m. Explain why the ball does not return to its starting height.
items.answer: At the bounce some energy is dissipated as thermal energy (and sound), so the ball has less energy and less gravitational potential energy at the top.
items.markingKey: energy transferred to thermal / sound [1]; less GPE so lower height [1] [2]

items.stem: Nadia drops a golf ball from a height of 2 m. It bounces back up to 1.2 m. (a) Describe the energy changes from the moment of release to the top of the bounce. (b) The gravitational potential energy is proportional to height. Calculate the percentage of the original energy the ball still has at the top of the bounce.
items.answer: (a) Gravitational potential → kinetic as it falls; at impact some kinetic is dissipated as thermal and sound, and some stored as elastic energy then back to kinetic; kinetic → gravitational potential as it rises. (b) 1.2 ÷ 2 × 100 = 60%
items.markingKey: (a) GPE → KE [1]; dissipation at bounce [1] (b) 1.2 ÷ 2 × 100 = 60% [1] [3]

items.stem: A loudspeaker is supplied with 800 J of electrical energy and transfers 40 J as useful sound. (a) Calculate the energy dissipated. (b) Calculate the percentage of the input energy that is useful.
Explain how a vacuum flask keeps a drink hot.
items.answer: The vacuum stops conduction and convection; the silvered walls reflect infrared radiation back; the stopper reduces convection and evaporation.
items.markingKey: vacuum stops conduction and convection [1]; silvered surface reduces radiation [1] [2]

items.stem: Freya says: "A metal bench feels colder than a wooden bench because the metal is at a lower temperature." Explain why Freya is wrong.
items.answer: Both are at the same temperature; metal is a better conductor so it takes energy from your hand faster, making it feel colder.
items.markingKey: same temperature [1]; metal conducts energy away faster [1] [2]

items.stem: Mohammed fills three identical metal cans, painted different colours, with water at 85 °C. After 10 minutes the temperatures are: dull black can: 65 °C, shiny white can: 74 °C, shiny silver can: 78 °C. Calculate the fall in temperature of the dull black can and state which surface emits radiation best.
items.answer: 20 °C; dull black

items.stem: Jonas is designing a cool box to keep drinks cold at a beach in Manila. (a) Suggest a material for the walls and explain your choice. (b) Suggest a colour for the outside of the box and explain why. (c) Explain why ice packs are best placed at the top of the box.
items.answer: (a) Polystyrene foam: it traps air, a poor conductor, and the air cannot form convection currents. (b) White or shiny: it reflects infrared radiation from the Sun, so less energy is absorbed. (c) Air cooled by the ice becomes denser and sinks, so convection currents carry cold air down over the drinks.
items.markingKey: (a) foam / trapped air [1]; poor conductor / no convection [1] [2] (b) white / shiny [1]; reflects radiation [1] [2] (c) cold air denser, sinks [1]; convection cools all drinks [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why sweating does not cool you as well on a very humid day.
items.answer: The air already contains a lot of water vapour, so sweat evaporates slowly and less energy is removed.
items.markingKey: humid air / much vapour [1]; slower evaporation [1] [2]

items.stem: Omar places two thermometers in a room at 30 °C. The bulb of thermometer B is wrapped in cotton wool soaked in water; thermometer A is dry. After 5 minutes A reads 30 °C and B reads 25 °C. A fan is then switched on and B falls to 22 °C. Calculate the extra cooling caused by the fan and explain it.
items.answer: 3 °C; the moving air removes vapour so the water evaporates faster, removing energy faster.
items.markingKey: 8 − 5 = 3 °C [1]; faster evaporation in moving air [1] [2]

items.stem: In hot, dry areas near Nairobi, people keep vegetables in a “pot-in-pot” cooler: a small clay pot inside a larger one, with wet sand between them. On a day at 35 °C, the inner pot stays at about 21 °C. (a) Explain why the cooler works better in dry air than in humid air. (b) Explain why the cooler must be refilled with water regularly.
items.answer: (a) Dry air contains little water vapour so evaporation is faster, giving more cooling. (b) Water is continually lost by evaporation; without water no evaporation, so no cooling.
items.markingKey: (a) dry air faster evaporation [1]; more cooling [1] [2] (b) water evaporates away [1]; no water no cooling [1] [2]
